claims.claim: Planar two-exit instances admit a cyclic two-gate decomposition. Let the exits be p,q and let B=N(p)∩N(q). Every component of G−({p,q}∪B) is adjacent to at most two vertices of B; when |B|≥3, those two are consecutive in the cyclic order of B around the exits.
claims.evidence: For k=|B|≥3, the inherited plane embedding of the K_{2,k} skeleton is simple, bipartite, and 2-connected. It has V=k+2, E=2k, and hence F=k. Every facial boundary has length at least four while their total length is 2E=4k, so every face is a 4-cycle p-b_i-q-b_{i+1}-p. An outside component together with its open attachment-edge interiors is connected and disjoint from the skeleton, hence lies in one open face and can meet only that face's two consecutive gates. For k≤2 the bound is immediate.
claims.witness: The exhaustive small-graph check examined all 16,384 simple graphs on six labeled vertices; every one of the 96 graphs having an outside component attached to at least three common gates contained a Kuratowski minor and was nonplanar.
claims.search_method: Direct Euler/topological proof, supplemented by exhaustive finite graph enumeration and exact minor testing.

claims.claim: All simple two-exit instances with at most one common exit-neighbor are linearly solvable, without assuming planarity. Put U=(N(p)∪N(q))−{p,q} and B=N(p)∩N(q). A start in {p,q}∪U wins. Otherwise, if B is empty the fugitive loses; if B={b}, let K be the component of b in G[U], and the fugitive wins exactly when N(s)∩K is nonempty.
claims.evidence: If s enters K immediately, fix a simple U-path to b. Every pre-b vertex on that path has exactly one exit edge; on arrival that edge is untouched, and Nemesis must delete it or lose next move. Thus every later path edge and both exit edges at b survive until b is reached, where one exit edge necessarily survives the response. Conversely, with B empty Nemesis deletes the sole exit edge at each newly reached boundary vertex. With B={b} and no first move into K, every route to K gives Nemesis a response at an outside-U position, or at a boundary vertex whose exit edge is already gone, on which she prepares b. Thereafter every regular vertex has at most one surviving exit edge; deleting that edge when present and otherwise the traversed edge prevents escape. All required sets and components are computable by adjacency scans.
claims.witness: Exact minimax agreed with the classification on 74,868 graph/start instances through six vertices, without a planarity restriction.
claims.search_method: Forced-response invariant plus exhaustive exact move-then-delete minimax.

claims.claim: There is a linear-time classification when the exits have the same independent neighborhood. After deleting a possible irrelevant edge pq, suppose N(p)=N(q)=B and B is independent. The fugitive wins exactly when (i) s∈{p,q}∪B, (ii) s has a neighbor in B, or (iii) s has a neighbor w having two distinct neighbors in B.
claims.evidence: In the ambient source domain of planar simple two-exit graphs, sufficiency is immediate: condition (iii) supplies two edge-disjoint three-edge gate configurations, so the first response can spoil at most one. For necessity, claim 0 gives at most two boundary gates per outside component. After the first move, Nemesis prepares the sole gate visible from the current vertex, or an arbitrary boundary gate. A move within the component gives another response before any second gate can be entered, allowing it to be prepared. Entering a prepared gate lets Nemesis delete its remaining exit edge. Since B is independent, departure from a dead gate enters an outside component for which the dead gate consumes one of the two boundary positions, leaving at most one new gate to prepare. This induction prevents entry into an unprepared gate. The three conditions are testable in O(V+E).
claims.witness: Exact minimax matched the characterization on 91,904 same-neighborhood/independent-B graph/start instances through five regular vertices. A separate nonplanar stress test produced a counterexample containing a K_{3,3} minor, confirming that the ambient planarity assumption used by this claim is essential.
claims.search_method: Planar two-gate induction, exhaustive finite minimax, and an adversarial scope stress test.

claims.claim: Two broader target-relevant subclasses are linearly solvable: (a) the graph induced by regular vertices is a forest, with arbitrary degrees; or (b) every regular vertex has degree at most three, with arbitrary exit degrees.
claims.evidence: Replace each regular-exit incidence by an edge to a distinct degree-one exit leaf. For every deleted-edge set and regular position, a path to an original exit exists exactly when a path to a replacement leaf exists, and moves and deletions correspond incidence-by-incidence. In case (a), each relevant transformed component is a tree. In case (b), every transformed vertex has degree at most three. The source's linear-time theorem therefore applies, and the transformation has linear size.
claims.witness: Outcome equivalence before and after exit splitting was exhaustively checked on 1,604 regular-start instances through five original vertices.
claims.search_method: Exact state-preserving reduction to the source's tree/maximum-degree-three theorem, supplemented by exhaustive minimax comparison.

claims.claim: The binary-escape-tree condition is not necessary even for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits. A seven-vertex counterexample has exits p,q, start s, regular vertices a,b,c,z, and edges pa,pb,qa,qb,ab,az,bz,bc,cz,cs.
claims.evidence: The graph is planar by embedding the four internally disjoint a-b paths ab, a-p-b, a-q-b, and a-z-b consecutively, then placing triangle b-c-z beside bz and attaching s at c. For the game, play s-c. If bc is deleted, play c-z; the edge-disjoint configurations {za,ap,aq} and {zb,bp,bq} ensure one complete gate survives the next deletion. Otherwise play c-b. If neither exit edge at b survives, the first two deletions were exactly bp and bq, leaving ab,ap,aq intact, so play through a. After exit splitting, s has degree one. A tree rooted at c must use b and z as children; with parent c, z must use a and b, repeating b across the two root branches. Hence neither possible root satisfies the tree condition.
claims.witness: Exact minimax returns a fugitive win; exact Kuratowski-minor exclusion certifies planarity; exhaustive subgraph search finds no binary escape tree rooted at s or c after splitting.
claims.search_method: Explicit strategy and embedding argument, independently checked by exhaustive minimax, minor testing, and binary-tree-subgraph enumeration.

claims.claim: The maximum-degree-three boundary for necessity of the binary-escape-tree condition is sharp even for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits. An eight-vertex witness has exits p,q, start s, other regular vertices c,a,b,x,z, and edges pa,pb,pz,qa,qb,sc,ca,cx,az,bx,bz,xz. It has maximum degree four; the fugitive wins, but after standard exit splitting neither s nor its only neighbor c roots a binary escape tree.
claims.evidence: The degrees are exactly (3,2,1,3,4,4,3,4). The supplied rotation system has six face orbits of lengths 3,3,3,4,4,7, giving 8−12+6=2 and therefore a sphere embedding. The stated strategy is exhaustive: after s-c, if ca survives, use a; loss of both a-exit edges consumes the first two deletions, leaving the z-b backup. If ca was deleted, use x; either the intact b configuration wins, or that second deletion leaves the z-p/a backup intact. After splitting, a tree rooted at c must branch to a and x; x must branch to b and z. Avoiding z forces a to use its two exit leaves, after which z has only its p-leaf available because a and b already occur elsewhere. Thus no full binary tree exists. Together with the source necessity theorem through degree three, this makes degree four sharp.
claims.witness: Exact minimax confirms the win, the rotation system certifies planarity, and exhaustive search over all split-graph edge subsets finds no binary escape tree rooted at s or c.
claims.search_method: Rotation-system verification, exact minimax, degree calculation, and exhaustive binary-tree-subgraph search.

claims.claim: With r regular vertices, the unrestricted two-exit game is outcome-equivalent to an r-move horizon recurrence. For regular v set W_0(D,v)=false; for t≥1, W_t(D,v) holds exactly when some surviving move vw either reaches an exit or has the property that, for every surviving edge e Nemesis might delete, w remains connected to an exit in G−(D∪{e}) and W_{t−1}(D∪{e},w) holds. A regular start s wins exactly when W_r(∅,s) holds.
claims.evidence: Induction on t gives the recurrence's exact bounded-horizon meaning and correct move/delete quantifier order. For the horizon, define ℓ(H,v) as the least forced escape time. Restoring edges cannot increase ℓ: by horizon induction, if Nemesis deletes a restored edge, compare the actual successor with a virtual successor obtained by deleting any surviving old edge; the actual graph is a supergraph. Along an ℓ-optimal strategy every nonterminal response strictly reduces ℓ. Revisiting v later in a subgraph H′ would give ℓ(H′,v)<ℓ(H,v), while restoration monotonicity gives ℓ(H,v)≤ℓ(H′,v), a contradiction. A winning play therefore visits no regular vertex twice and reaches an exit in at most r moves.
claims.witness: Unrestricted exact minimax and W_r agreed on all 548 simple two-exit graphs through five vertices, across all 1,604 regular starts.
claims.search_method: Induction, rank/restoration monotonicity proof, and exhaustive comparison of independent recurrences.

claims.claim: The horizon recurrence gives an exact O*((27/4)^r)-time algorithm for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits, where r is the number of regular vertices, and depth-first evaluation establishes PSPACE membership.
claims.evidence: At deletion depth i, t=r−i, so a memoized state is determined by a deletion set D of size i and one of r regular positions. Thus there are at most r·Σ_{i=0}^r C(m,i) states, with polynomial transition work. After ignoring pq, a planar simple graph on r+2 vertices has m≤3r. For i≤r, 1≤2^r·2^(−i), hence Σ_{i=0}^r C(m,i)≤2^rΣ_i C(m,i)2^(−i)≤2^r(3/2)^m≤(27/4)^r. Depth-first evaluation has depth at most r and stores only polynomial-size masks, counters, positions, and iteration frames, proving polynomial space.
claims.witness: The exact integer inequality Σ_{i=0}^r C(m,i)≤(27/4)^r was checked for all 9,800 pairs 1≤r≤80 and 0≤m≤3r; the displayed binomial-theorem argument covers every r.
claims.search_method: Symbolic state counting and binomial weighting, supplemented by exact arbitrary-precision integer checks.

target_evidence: The source target requires either a polynomial-time classification for every planar simple graph with exactly two exits or a matching hardness result. The draft explicitly supplies neither: O*((27/4)^r) remains exponential because r can grow linearly with the input. Its verified decompositions, subclasses, counterexamples, exact recurrence, and improved exponential algorithm are nevertheless material target-relevant progress. Calling the result PARTIAL is therefore accurate.
